points.requirement: **Assume** one hypothetical tissue element receives each listed fraction, with negligible repair during delivery and complete repair of modeled sublethal damage between fractions. This expression omits repopulation and overall treatment time; it cannot automatically describe prolonged or internally distributed irradiation. Use **3 Gy and 10 Gy as alternative assumed α/β values**, not measurements of a person's tumor or organs. By radiobiology convention, about 10 Gy stands for tumors and early-responding tissues such as skin and mucosa, and about 3 Gy for late-responding normal tissues. Breast cancer is an exception: the START trials estimated α/β at 4.6 Gy (95% confidence interval 1.1–8.1) for tumor control and 3.4 Gy (2.3–4.5) for late change in breast appearance. The trialists read this as breast cancer and its dose-limiting normal tissues responding similarly to fraction size. See the [International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) model equation](https://pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Pub1556_web.pdf#page=84).

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The linear-quadratic model expresses the surviving cell fraction after dose d as exp(-alpha × d - beta × d squared). The alpha/beta ratio is a parameter in gray for a specified tissue and endpoint. At fixed total physical dose, a lower ratio gives fraction size greater weight. Historical teaching values near ten gray for many tumours and early-responding tissues such as skin and mucosa, and three for late normal-tissue effects, are conventions rather than constants for every tumour or organ. A planned START-A/pilot meta-analysis estimated 4.6 gray for breast tumour control, with 95% confidence interval 1.1 to 8.1, and 3.4 for late photographic breast change, interval 2.3 to 4.5. The trialists interpreted these estimates as similar fraction-size sensitivity for breast cancer and its dose-limiting normal tissues.

The basic equal-fraction calculation assumes equal effects per fraction and complete repair between fractions and does not include overall treatment time. Too short an interval or slow repair can violate that assumption. Extrapolation to a large fraction size or prolonged irradiation needs assessment; a model calculation alone validates neither the pattern nor clinical equivalence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The linear-quadratic model expresses the surviving cell fraction after dose d as exp(-alpha × d - beta × d squared). The alpha/beta ratio is a parameter in gray for a specified tissue and endpoint. At fixed total physical dose, a lower ratio gives fraction size greater weight. Historical teaching values near ten gray for many tumours and early-responding tissues such as skin and mucosa, and three for late normal-tissue effects, are conventions rather than constants for every tumour or organ. A planned START-A/pilot meta-analysis estimated 4.6 gray for breast tumour control, with 95% confidence interval 1.1 to 8.1, and 3.4 for late photographic breast change, interval 2.3 to 4.5. The trialists interpreted these estimates as similar fraction-size sensitivity for breast cancer and its dose-limiting normal tissues.

The basic equal-fraction calculation assumes equal effects per fraction and complete repair between fractions and does not include overall treatment time. Too short an interval or slow repair can violate that assumption. Extrapolation to a large fraction size or prolonged irradiation needs assessment; a model calculation alone validates neither the pattern nor clinical equivalence.

Stereotactic body radiotherapy, also called SABR, uses specialised localisation, planning, positioning, image guidance and delivery to give a high dose per fraction to a body target outside the brain. A small number of visits does not establish that this delivery package was used. A biologically effective dose calculation compares modelled effects under assumptions; it does not document stereotactic localisation, motion management or verification. Modern non-stereotactic radiotherapy can also use imaging, conformal beams and motion assessment.

The target, motion, dose distribution, positioning uncertainty, prior overlapping radiation and normal-organ constraints determine the coverage problem. Dose falls through space rather than stopping at a drawn line. There is no universal one-centimetre safe boundary, lesion-size ceiling or prescription that applies to every organ. Planned exposure, verified delivery, local control and toxicity need their own measurements.

A 2010 prospective study concerned medically inoperable peripheral early-stage lung cancer and measured local control, distant failure and toxicity. That setting does not validate treatment of every central lesion or organ. CURB and NRG-BR002 tested different metastatic settings and comparisons. Local control, added progression-free or overall survival, symptom relief and an immune response are separate outcomes.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
The 2020 consensus defines immunogenic cell death through the adaptive immune response, not merely the appearance of dead cells. Antigens, appropriately timed danger signals, antigen-presenting cells and a responsive host all matter. Apoptotic or other death machinery does not by itself classify the immune outcome.

Calreticulin exposure, ATP or HMGB1 release and interferon-related signals are useful mechanistic readouts, but none alone proves protective immunity. Functional cross-priming and appropriate in-vivo immune tests address later steps. The consensus distinguishes mouse vaccination models from established disease; neither a surrogate marker nor a positive mouse assay establishes clinical benefit in a person.

points.heading: Common failure modes
points.requirement: Do not infer universal superiority of freezing over heating from antigen-preservation arguments. The BOOSTER lung-cancer report claims, from a subgroup analysis, that cryoablation (13 patients) gave longer progression-free survival than thermal ablation (31 patients). Its randomization compared ablation with no ablation, so the freeze-versus-heat comparison is nonrandomized and small; it generates a hypothesis rather than a ranking. Do not equate higher dose with greater immune learning. Do not assume an [immune-checkpoint inhibitor](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/immunotherapy/immune-checkpoint-inhibitor) repairs every missing recognition step. Compare complete strategies in matching populations rather than ranking tools by a single mechanism.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: BOOSTER randomised 65 selected patients with residual advanced lung cancer after checkpoint treatment, rather than the planned 137; its primary analysis included 42 with ablation and twenty without. The primary progression-free-survival clock began at immunotherapy initiation, before randomisation, so its medians of 26.7 versus 11.7 months include a selected pre-entry period. The report separately gives a randomisation-clock analysis of 17.1 versus 4.4 months. These clocks cannot be exchanged when comparing headlines. The physician selected freezing or heating: the abstract says thirteen cryoablation and 31 thermal-ablation patients, whereas Figure 3 and the discussion say thirteen and 29 among the 42 analysed. The discussion also notes larger lesions in the thermal group and no correction for multiple comparisons. This internally discrepant, exploratory comparison does not establish universal superiority of freezing or an immune-optimal modality.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: The strategy uses relevant tumour antigens in place while supporting presenting cells and immune activation. Antigen availability, uptake and processing, cross-presentation, suitable priming, access to another lesion, recognition of naturally displayed targets and useful function are conditional jobs. Local injury can supply material without establishing all these steps, and danger signals alone do not establish immunogenic cell death. An uninjected lesion can still be exposed to systemic drugs.

points.heading: What each measurement can contribute
points.requirement: For [target PET and theranostic imaging](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/imaging/target-pet-and-theranostic-imaging), record the tracer, binding component and radionuclide; [immuno-PET](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/imaging/immuno-pet) uses a radiolabeled antibody or antibody-derived fragment. For a [radioligand](/wiki/education/guides/local-therapy-and-the-immune-system/06-comparisons), a diagnostic image does not substitute for dosimetry, which estimates absorbed radiation dose and normal-organ exposure product by product. Joint guidance from the European Association of Nuclear Medicine and the Medical Internal Radiation Dose Committee describes quantitative imaging for dosimetry of lutetium-177 therapies; that method scope does not establish any treatment's benefit in breast cancer. [Ljungberg and colleagues, 2016](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26471692/).

points.entailment: The binder/fragment, radionuclide and product are explicit. Quantitative lutetium-177 guidance concerns a method, not breast-cancer benefit; uptake/retention and normal-organ dose remain product-specific.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
Immuno-PET uses radiolabelled antibodies or antibody-derived binders. Full immunoglobulin G (IgG), antigen-binding fragments (Fab), minibodies and single-domain nanobodies differ in size and pharmacokinetics. The format can affect penetration, clearance, retention and normal-organ background; there is no universal best format. A label makes the binder traceable, not a perfect detector of every target site.

The radionuclide must suit the product's imaging time course. Dijkers' 89Zr-trastuzumab study examined a full antibody over several days; Keyaerts' 68Ga-HER2 nanobody study imaged at earlier times. These are product-specific examples. Antibody imaging can concern a tumour-associated target or immune cells. CD8 binder imaging belongs here; granzyme-B peptide or peptidomimetic imaging is a different tracer class and has its own record.

Background in blood and normal organs, lesion size and clearance affect interpretation. One image cannot isolate every delivery, binding and retention contribution, quantify receptor occupancy or supply a therapeutic absorbed dose. Protein mass is not a target-positive cell fraction, and uptake is not an expression percentage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Calibrated activity measurements, often from suitable serial SPECT or PET imaging, inform a time-activity model. Time-integrated decays, emission properties, tissue mass and spatial assumptions then inform absorbed dose. Equal uptake on an early scan can be followed by different retention and different doses. Administered activity is an input, not a substitute for patient- or tissue-level dosimetry. The estimates can support evaluation of dosing strategies, but improved outcomes from a particular adaptation require their own evidence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Absorbed dose in gray (Gy) is energy deposited per tissue mass, with 1 Gy equal to 1 joule per kilogram. Administered activity in MBq measures radioactive decays per time, not energy absorbed. A single uptake image or SUV is neither quantity. Dose estimation needs an appropriate time-activity model, emissions and energy-deposition assumptions for the relevant tissue. Equal early uptake can precede different retention. The tested diagnostic tracer cannot supply a different therapeutic product's dose merely because both bind the same target.

points.entailment: The reviewed image means sectioning/extraction consume material; shapes/amounts are schematic and diagnostic needs and method input govern allocation. This remains peer-proposal text, not an integrated graph image or standard amount.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Cutting sections moves material from the block onto slides; extraction consumes a portion and loses its original architecture. Stored images and datasets can be copied and reanalysed but cannot refill the archive. A newly collected biopsy is another procedure and time point, and a growing culture is a changed system rather than replenishment of the original specimen.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Specimen allocation starts by identifying the available portions, assessing their suitability, estimating method-specific use and recording consumption. Blocks, slides, frozen pieces and cell aliquots are finite inputs; their counts alone do not establish adequacy. Record remaining portions with section thickness, area or analyte amounts and the relevant context. Receiving-laboratory requirements and diagnostic priorities apply, rather than a universal test budget. Outdated inventories, unrecognised exhaustion, unsuitable regions and duplicated destructive work can waste material. Specimen governance supports reliable testing but is not itself a clinical biomarker and does not establish whether a test changes care or another procedure is appropriate.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Keep physical portions and their custody separate from reusable data. The record links collection site and time, treatment context, preparation, represented region and cells, prior use, remainder, holder and permitted use. Permission to analyse a dataset does not itself permit transferring or consuming its source block. For an authorised physical use, track the portion, sender, recipient, handling, receipt, consumption and remainder at each handoff. A returned block does not restore cut or extracted material. Diagnostic evaluation, patient safety and applicable consent take priority; the receiving laboratory and pathology must resolve actual suitability rather than infer it from quantity alone. Before allocation, specify the question, receiving method, minimum usable input, processing and transport timing, assay controls and what remains for other needs. These are method-specific requirements rather than a universal number of biopsy cores.

[Fixed, fresh-frozen and viable preparations](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/specimens/ffpe-vs-fresh-frozen-vs-viable) support different questions, so the first allocation question is not "is there tissue left?" but "does this assay accept *this* material?" A label such as “frozen” cannot guarantee living cells or compatibility.

points.heading: How tissue planning changes the answer
points.requirement: Some frozen tissues yield nuclei without yielding recoverable living cells, which is why [single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/transcriptomics/single-cell-and-single-nucleus-rna-seq) need different preparation plans and capture different cell populations ([Slyper et al., 2020](https://www.broadinstitute.org/publications/broad630206)). A large tumor bed may also contain scar, normal tissue and immune cells, so quantity alone does not identify the cells a question needs.

sourceRefs.exactPassage: Some frozen tissues yield nuclei without yielding recoverable living cells, which is why [single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/transcriptomics/single-cell-and-single-nucleus-rna-seq) need different preparation plans and capture different cell populations ([Slyper et al., 2020](https://www.broadinstitute.org/publications/broad630206)). A large tumor bed may also contain scar, normal tissue and immune cells, so quantity alone does not identify the cells a question needs.

points.entailment: Slyper fresh-cell/frozen-nucleus workflows can recover similar types at differing proportions; a mixed tumour bed or a frozen label cannot establish malignant content, living-cell recovery or assay suitability.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A tumour specimen can contain malignant, immune, stromal and normal cells. A difference in an aggregate molecular signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells or both. That is different from a directly counted cell fraction or a density per sampled area, each of which also needs its denominator and sampled region.

Preparation can change what is recovered. Slyper and colleagues compared single-cell and single-nucleus profiling in matched tumour specimens and found similar cell types at sometimes different proportions. A recovered profile mixture is therefore not automatically the original tissue census. Deconvolution and purity models can help investigate contributions under assumptions; they do not certify the cell of origin of every signal or remove sampling differences.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Slyper's 2020 tumour toolbox used single-cell profiling for fresh material and single-nucleus profiling for frozen material, with tissue-specific customisation. Matched preparations typically recovered similar cell types but sometimes different proportions. Some frozen specimens can supply nuclei without recoverable living cells, and neither preparation label guarantees a useful dataset. A new collection cannot recreate the original specimen's place and time; a successful model or molecular assay does not establish clinical treatment benefit.

points.heading: How tissue planning changes the answer
points.requirement: Record the physical material separately from the data it produced. **Custody** means who holds each portion and what happened at every handoff: site, collection time, treatment context, preparation, represented cells, prior use, remaining quantity, location and permitted use. Permission to analyze an existing dataset is not permission to consume the block, and "block returned" is not a record of what was cut or extracted from it.

Permission to analyze an existing dataset is not permission to consume the block, and "block returned" is not a record of what was cut or extracted from it.

points.entailment: The physical/data distinction, all handoff/context fields, diagnostic reserve/current region, data-versus-consumption permissions and consumption after block return are explicit.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Keep physical portions and their custody separate from reusable data. The record links collection site and time, treatment context, preparation, represented region and cells, prior use, remainder, holder and permitted use. Permission to analyse a dataset does not itself permit transferring or consuming its source block. For an authorised physical use, track the portion, sender, recipient, handling, receipt, consumption and remainder at each handoff. A returned block does not restore cut or extracted material. Diagnostic evaluation, patient safety and applicable consent take priority; the receiving laboratory and pathology must resolve actual suitability rather than infer it from quantity alone. Before allocation, specify the question, receiving method, minimum usable input, processing and transport timing, assay controls and what remains for other needs. These are method-specific requirements rather than a universal number of biopsy cores.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In an invented archive, one FFPE block came from a breast lesion collected on teaching day zero after systemic treatment. The last pathology review identified a mixed region of tumour, scar and immune cells. Diagnostic sections were cut earlier, but usable depth and relevant remainder are unknown. Pathology holds the block and must establish its diagnostic reserve; permission covers named molecular and image projects but no physical transfer. Lab A accepts FFPE and requests four five-micrometre sections: hold cutting until pathology confirms suitable remainder and the laboratory confirms input and permissions. Lab B requires living tumour cells: reject this fixed block for that request and ask which compatible input would be needed, without authorising another collection. The image team may reuse the already permitted teaching image version one from the last reviewed slide level without new cutting, recording its version and source slide. This is a complete allocation decision despite a named hold, not a standard section count or reserve percentage.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Delivery can be compared without ranking treatments. A fictional probe card controls a selected liver site, a beam card specifies a lung volume and motion assessment, and a radioactive-drug card requires distribution, retention and organ dosimetry. They are different routes, not a ladder from one lesion to invisible disease. A systemically distributed radioactive product still does not guarantee exposure of every microscopic deposit. Radiation injury does not require a conventional T cell to recognise peptide-HLA; proposed antigen-specific immune effects still need presentation, access, recognition and function. In another invented study, people receiving the same systemic strategy are randomised to a local addition or no local addition. With the same defined progression endpoint, starting time and follow-up, treated sites are controlled but new lesions occur in both arms and the progression-free-survival interval spans effects in both directions. That supports local control while leaving the added progression effect uncertain; survival, quality of life, pain and harms remain separate outcomes.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Questions follow the product. For a cytotoxic antibody-drug conjugate, assess antibody, linker and payload together, delivery and exposure, tested resistance steps and the design-specific role of internalisation; FDA's March 2024 clinical-pharmacology guidance has this scope. For an engager or cell product, ask about cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity and other neurologic effects, healthy-tissue recognition, tissue access and what can persist after dosing stops. FDA's January 2024 CAR T-cell guidance describes product-specific recognition, expansion, persistence and toxicity management; it does not supply incidence for every engager. For a radioligand, ask how the imaging relates to that therapeutic product's distribution, organ absorbed doses and organ limits. FDA's August 2019 document addresses nonclinical studies and labeling, not a universal clinical dose threshold. Tracer uptake supplies no CAR-T safety threshold. For a T-cell-receptor proposal, ask which peptide-HLA target is recognised and how specificity, natural presentation and function were tested; receptor sequences or expanded clones alone leave these questions open.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Now change only the fictional request: after complete tumour removal, someone proposes manufacturing Q and administering it to prevent recurrence because M RNA was abundant, an IND is said to be active and a supplier offers manufacture. The setting and commitments have changed, while the dossier is still one biopsy RNA signal plus cultured-cell activity. Neither that evidence nor the attributed investigational milestone or supply offer establishes postoperative benefit. Ask the clinical team for Q-specific human evidence or a relevant protocol, the sponsor which product and protocol are covered, and the readiness owner about delivery requirements. In the United States an effective Investigational New Drug application is not marketing approval, and submission of a Biologics License Application is not its approval. A manufacturing quote cannot confirm supply, consent, review, delivery and monitoring as a whole. With only this dossier, evidence and pathway review are justified; manufacture or administration is not justified by the supplied information. Speculative availability does not promise access or protection against recurrence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. Speculative availability does not promise access or protection against recurrence.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Specimen allocation starts by identifying the available portions, assessing their suitability, estimating method-specific use and recording consumption. Blocks, slides, frozen pieces and cell aliquots are finite inputs; their counts alone do not establish adequacy. Receiving-laboratory requirements and diagnostic priorities apply, rather than a universal test budget. coverageEvidence.excerpt: Specimen allocation starts by identifying the available portions, assessing their suitability, estimating method-specific use and recording consumption. Blocks, slides, frozen pieces and cell aliquots are finite inputs; their counts alone do not establish adequacy. Record remaining portions with section thickness, area or analyte amounts and the relevant context. Receiving-laboratory requirements and diagnostic priorities apply, rather than a universal test budget. Outdated inventories, unrecognised exhaustion, unsuitable regions and duplicated destructive work can waste material. Specimen governance supports reliable testing but is not itself a clinical biomarker and does not establish whether a test changes care or another procedure is appropriate.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: Keep physical portions and their custody separate from reusable data. The record links collection site and time, treatment context, preparation, represented region and cells, prior use, remainder, holder and permitted use. Permission to analyse a dataset does not itself permit transferring or consuming its source block. For an authorised physical use, track the portion, sender, recipient, handling, receipt, consumption and remainder at each handoff. A returned block does not restore cut or extracted material. Diagnostic evaluation, patient safety and applicable consent take priority; the receiving laboratory and pathology must resolve actual suitability rather than infer it from quantity alone. Before allocation, specify the question, receiving method, minimum usable input, processing and transport timing, assay controls and what remains for other needs. These are method-specific requirements rather than a universal number of biopsy cores.

points.requirement: **Everything in this scenario is fictional. The laboratory requirements and permissions are supplied assumptions, not standard section counts or clinical instructions.**

sourceRefs.exactPassage: **Everything in this scenario is fictional. The laboratory requirements and permissions are supplied assumptions, not standard section counts or clinical instructions.**

points.entailment: All archive premises remain explicitly fictional: breast lesion/day zero after systemic treatment, last reviewed mixed region, prior cuts/unknown usable depth, pathology reserve/holder, named molecular-image permission without transfer and image version/source slide. Historical review is not a claim about the current remainder.

coverageEvidence.excerpt: In an invented archive, one FFPE block came from a breast lesion collected on teaching day zero after systemic treatment. The last pathology review identified a mixed region of tumour, scar and immune cells. Diagnostic sections were cut earlier, but usable depth and relevant remainder are unknown. Pathology holds the block and must establish its diagnostic reserve; permission covers named molecular and image projects but no physical transfer. Lab A accepts FFPE and requests four five-micrometre sections: hold cutting until pathology confirms suitable remainder and the laboratory confirms input and permissions. Lab B requires living tumour cells: reject this fixed block for that request and ask which compatible input would be needed, without authorising another collection. The image team may reuse the already permitted teaching image version one from the last reviewed slide level without new cutting, recording its version and source slide. This is a complete allocation decision despite a named hold, not a standard section count or reserve percentage.

This simple cell fraction is not the clinical stromal tumour-infiltrating-lymphocyte score, which has a different denominator.

anchors.text:
Intratumoral describes a route into a tumour, while immunotherapy describes the intended immune-directed action. Products, injection methods and accompanying treatments differ. A lesion-based method needs an identified safely accessible site; local delivery does not guarantee confined exposure or systemic safety.

An in-situ vaccination strategy is one possible use of local tumour material, rather than a synonym for every injection. Evidence must distinguish injected-lesion changes, controlled immune assays, uninjected-lesion outcomes and the whole regimen’s benefits and harms.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: Intratumoral means within a tumour; intralesional means within a lesion. Intratumoral immunotherapy combines a route with an immune-directed treatment purpose. The name does not identify the substance, and a locally injected cytotoxic drug need not be immunotherapy. An in-situ vaccination strategy seeks useful immune learning from material in the body; it is not a synonym for every injection. Local-material and learning analogies leave direct drug effects and procedure risks unresolved.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: A lesion-based injection needs an identified site that can be reached safely by the specified method. The accessible lesion may not represent every other tumour site. Entry of a needle does not establish uniform distribution, confined exposure or systemic safety. Recruitment or activation of presenting cells, antigen collection and priming can be investigated, while travel to another lesion, natural recognition and sustained function remain separate questions. Inflammation, local injury, infection and systemic effects depend on the product and procedure.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: Keep three measurements separate. Changes in size or tissue at the injected lesion show local observations. Controlled assays of antigen-reactive cells ask an immune-response question but leave natural recognition and function elsewhere unresolved. Changes at uninjected lesions ask another question, while the injection's added effect and longer-term patient benefit need a suitable comparison. Report each component's route and serial injected and uninjected lesion results. An uninjected lesion can still receive systemic co-treatment, so it need not be untreated.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: The U.S. Imlygic label specifies talimogene laherparepvec for local treatment of unresectable cutaneous, subcutaneous and nodal melanoma lesions recurrent after initial surgery. It states that improved overall survival and an effect on visceral metastases have not been shown. A local melanoma indication does not establish whole-body benefit or a breast-cancer indication. Intralesional administration also does not remove the label's infection, wound and other product-specific precautions.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: In a fictional study, the injected lesion shrinks, a controlled immune assay becomes positive and a separate lesion stays unchanged. The observations establish local and assay activity under their stated definitions, without demonstrating distant control. The result also does not establish that no immune-learning event occurred. Testing naturally presenting targets, relevant function, later outcomes and harms addresses additional questions.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: For radiation, an abscopal effect describes an observation outside the irradiated field. After an injection, describe an uninjected-lesion response and name concurrent treatments before attributing it to the injection or to immunity. Marabelle's expert panel specifically distinguished injected from noninjected lesions because systemic co-treatment can expose both. A combination's name alone does not reveal which component was injected.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: Read the component list before interpreting a combination. Intratumoral means inside a tumour and intravenous means into a vein; an accompanying checkpoint antibody may have either route according to the protocol. Record the injected material and lesion, every systemic drug and its route, and any radiation or ablation. Electroporation uses electrical pulses to support entry into cells; the injected gene payload and electrical delivery are separate intervention components. Track lesions whose injection status changes over time. Product manufacture, dosing procedures, monitoring and subsequent surgery or care belong in the study plan; a registry listing establishes neither benefit, local availability nor eligibility. DCIS, invasive breast cancer and melanoma are different populations, and a preoperative pathological response is not a survival endpoint.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: In an invented single-arm study, twelve people each have an injected and an uninjected lesion, and all receive a systemic drug. At the stated assessment, injected-lesion responses occur in eight, uninjected-lesion responses in two and a defined blood immune-assay response in five. Each denominator is twelve, but participants can overlap: adding the counts to claim fifteen responders is invalid. These lesion counts do not provide the target-lesion, non-target and new-lesion information needed for a formal patient response category. Even all three observations in one person would not isolate the injection's contribution. Compare the combination with the same systemic treatment without the injected intervention, retaining population, endpoints, assessment timing, harms and appropriate control or blinding procedures.

anchors.text:
Responses at non-irradiated sites motivate investigation of immune effects of local radiation. Keep the irradiated and unirradiated lesions, other treatments and observation times explicit. A proposed immune mechanism needs more than local injury or circulating markers.

A case or uncontrolled combination cannot isolate the added effect of radiation. Comparative local-treatment studies must retain their populations and endpoints: a response outside the field, progression-free survival, overall survival and symptom relief are different outcomes.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: First define the irradiated field and the actual exposure of each lesion. A local response does not demonstrate a distant response. An uninjected-lesion response in an injection study is a different route-defined observation. During concurrent systemic treatment, distant shrinkage does not by itself isolate radiation’s contribution or demonstrate immune causation; local control, distant response, survival, symptoms and harms require separate assessment.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: To assess a distant effect, retain lesion exposure, serial imaging, prespecified response rules, timing and concurrent therapies. Report lesion changes separately from patient response proportions and their eligible denominators. Imaging is an input; optional tissue and immune tests use finite samples. Exposure misclassification, missing assessments, selected evaluable groups and concurrent-drug attribution can distort interpretation. There is no universal abscopal cutoff or percentage across cancers and regimens; case observations, model mechanisms and comparative clinical outcomes are different evidence tiers.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: In a fictional combination study, an irradiated site is controlled while a lesion outside the field shrinks during systemic therapy. The observation is a distant response under that treatment context. It does not prove that radiation vaccinated the whole body, establish which component caused it or supply a general response frequency. Test exposure, relevant comparisons and the proposed immune mechanism separately.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: Ho's single-arm phase 2 study combined radiation with pembrolizumab in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. The week-13 unirradiated-lesion endpoint yielded three responses among seventeen enrolled people, 17.6%, with a 95% confidence interval of 4.7% to 44.2%. Eight died from progression before week 13; among the nine assessed then, the same three responses were 33.3%, rounded to one decimal place. These are different denominators for the same numerator, not two treatment effects. Without a randomised systemic-treatment-only group, neither proportion estimates what radiation added or supplies a general abscopal probability.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text:
Surgery, ablation and external radiation address defined tissues, while systemically administered medicines and radiopharmaceuticals distribute more broadly. Regional delivery has an intermediate anatomical scope. Distribution, effective exposure and benefit are separate questions; neither local nor systemic is a guarantee of complete cellular coverage.

Local control, distant progression, progression-free survival, overall survival and symptom relief should be measured separately. A null added-survival comparison does not make palliation irrelevant, and a controlled treated site does not establish control throughout the body. Compare the actual complete strategies rather than assuming that adding a local method always improves outcomes.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: BOOSTER studied ablation during ongoing immunotherapy after limited residual lung disease; CURB studied SBRT for oligoprogression in lung and breast cohorts; NRG-BR002 studied ablation during first-line systemic treatment for limited metastatic breast cancer. PACIFIC tested consolidation durvalumab after concurrent chemoradiotherapy in nonprogressing stage III lung cancer. These are distinct settings and intervention contrasts.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: Start with the goal and history before choosing a clock. A smaller lesion is a response observation at assessment; local control concerns keeping that site from progressing during follow-up. Postoperative local-recurrence prevention, relief of pain from a bone metastasis and a growing lesion during otherwise controlled metastatic disease are different questions. A meaningful pain improvement need not wait for an untreated tumour to shrink. A positive blood molecular test does not identify a lesion's position, boundary or safe access. An earlier scan date alone does not demonstrate improved outcomes. These distinctions organise evidence review rather than select a dose, procedure or treatment date. Nonmetastatic disease means no established distant metastases; a stage and subtype still need their own comparison of local and systemic care. Recovery, healing, previous exposure, overlapping toxicities and protocol assessment times supply other clocks. They are reasons to examine the studied sequence rather than invent a universal interval or repeat a procedure whenever a blood marker rises.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: A local-treatment proposal needs five connected answers: the local and hoped-for wider outcomes with their measurements; evidence matching the cancer, disease history, complete strategy and comparator; access, intended coverage, margins, motion and nearby structures; actual exposure and normal-tissue risk; and alternatives, burdens and remaining uncertainty. In a fictional pair of equally sized lesions, proximity to a sensitive airway and a different approach can change feasibility. Depth alone is also insufficient: some deep lesions can be accessed, while a superficial lesion can have a difficult margin. Small diameter and a positive tracer scan settle none of the wider immune or outcome claims. Comparators can include systemic treatment alone, another local strategy, observation where appropriate or a study; include visits, recovery and additional sampling among the burdens. For a tracer and therapeutic product, establish the relationship between them rather than treating target uptake as a measured therapeutic dose. This review identifies missing facts and does not authorise treatment.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: Delivery can be compared without ranking treatments. A fictional probe card controls a selected liver site, a beam card specifies a lung volume and motion assessment, and a radioactive-drug card requires distribution, retention and organ dosimetry. They are different routes, not a ladder from one lesion to invisible disease. A systemically distributed radioactive product still does not guarantee exposure of every microscopic deposit. Radiation injury does not require a conventional T cell to recognise peptide-HLA; proposed antigen-specific immune effects still need presentation, access, recognition and function. In another invented study, people receiving the same systemic strategy are randomised to a local addition or no local addition. With the same defined progression endpoint, starting time and follow-up, treated sites are controlled but new lesions occur in both arms and the progression-free-survival interval spans effects in both directions. That supports local control while leaving the added progression effect uncertain; survival, quality of life, pain and harms remain separate outcomes.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: PACIFIC's five-year report concerns durvalumab versus placebo after concurrent platinum-based chemoradiation in unresectable, nonprogressing stage III non-small-cell lung cancer. The report found sustained progression-free and overall-survival benefit for that tested consolidation strategy. It did not require stereotactic body radiation, identify an abscopal mechanism or establish that focused radiation should always precede checkpoint treatment across cancers. Randomised comparisons, development phase and publication format answer different questions; these study cards cannot rank technologies from separate headlines. A case can describe a clinical course, a nonrandomised comparison can be distorted by treatment selection, and a model can supply a rationale for testing. These designs do not establish the same causal claim.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text:
Oligoprogression describes limited progression within otherwise controlled metastatic disease during treatment. It is not restricted to one or two lesions or to targeted pills: the number, imaging rules and prior treatment depend on the definition being used. Oligometastatic disease describes limited detected distant spread, while limited residual disease describes what remains after treatment; retain the earlier burden and whether the remaining lesions are growing.

Treating progressing sites while continuing systemic therapy is a strategy to evaluate, rather than an automatic instruction. CURB tested adding stereotactic body radiation to standard care in lung and breast cohorts with different results. A current lesion count cannot establish benefit, safety or which systemic treatment should continue.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: CURB was an open-label randomised phase 2 study after at least first-line systemic treatment, defining oligoprogression as at most five progressive lesions on CT or PET-CT. The prespecified lung cohort had median progression-free survival of 10.0 months with SBRT plus standard care versus 2.2 with standard care, hazard ratio 0.41, 95% confidence interval 0.22 to 0.75. The breast cohort had 4.4 versus 4.2 months, hazard ratio 0.78, interval 0.43 to 1.43. Failure to show a breast-cohort improvement does not establish an exact zero effect or a precise effect in every breast subtype. The intervention, comparator and harms must stay with the population.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: In two fictional current scan reports, each maps two lesions. Card A previously had eight before checkpoint treatment and now has two nongrowing residual lesions; card B had two during systemic treatment and now has one growing while the other remains controlled. A poses a limited-residual-disease question and B a limited-progression question. Equal current counts do not make the histories interchangeable or establish trial eligibility, an optimal procedure or a timing rule. BOOSTER studied a response-selected residual lung-cancer setting; CURB selected progression after systemic treatment.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text:
Oligometastatic disease describes limited detected distant spread, under a specified clinical or study definition. It is a hypothesis that some limited patterns may be amenable to treatment directed at all visible sites; a few visible lesions do not prove a distinct biology or the absence of microscopic disease. Regional lymph nodes alone are not distant metastases.

The ESTRO-ASTRO consensus describes one to five lesions, with every site safely treatable, while acknowledging that there is no universally established maximum. A consensus definition is not proof of added benefit. Treatment decisions require the cancer setting, prior burden and treatment, comparator, endpoint, safety and the person's goals.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: A few lit windows show what is detectable, not a census of every room. This analogy does not mean that every limited pattern conceals widespread disease. Synchronous metastases are detected near the initial diagnosis; metachronous metastases are detected later, with the interval defined by the author or protocol. Induced limited disease follows previously widespread disease and systemic treatment. Oligoprogression means a growing subset while other disease remains controlled during treatment. Limited residual or persistent disease means limited visible disease remains after treatment; specify whether it is stable or progressing. These labels are not universal synonyms.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: NRG-BR002 tested adding ablation to first-line systemic therapy in breast cancer with at most four metastases, controlled primary disease, at most 12 months of first-line therapy without progression, and all visible sites amenable to SBRT or resection. Of 129 enrolled patients, 125 were eligible for analysis and 79% had HR-positive/HER2-negative disease. In the protocol-specified phase 2 go/no-go analysis with a December 20, 2021 data cutoff, median progression-free survival was 23.0 months without ablation and 19.5 months with it; the hazard ratio was 0.92, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.57 to 1.47 and stratified P = .42. Overall survival did not differ significantly and the study did not proceed to phase 3. This does not supply a definitive effect for every subtype or erase a separate symptom-relief goal.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: Classification uses the imaging and its coverage and sensitivity, lesion and organ counts, locations, sizes, dates, previous burden, systemic treatment and response or progression history. A biopsy may be needed to confirm a finding, but classification is not inherently a tumour-consuming molecular assay. Benign mimics, undetected lesions and missing earlier records can mislead. Keep a protocol's count, timing, primary-control and treatability requirements; five lesions is not a cure cutoff and a molecular result does not universally establish this state.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: Three fictional histories can each contain two lesions now: two newly detected metastases with no earlier distant disease, two residual lesions after treatment of many, or two growing sites amid many stable sites during therapy. The numeral counts a different subset in each history. Keep the earlier burden and dates rather than merging these groups. A response-selected group and a progression-selected group answer different questions; curative intent is a documented goal whose success needs long-term outcome measurement, not an inference from the current count.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: NRG-BR002's accessible NIH author manuscript distinguishes its protocol-specified phase 2 analysis from non-protocol-specified extended follow-up with a September 4, 2025 cutoff. The latter reported median progression-free survival of 23.0 months without ablation versus 29.5 with it, hazard ratio 0.93, 95% confidence interval 0.60 to 1.44, and overall-survival hazard ratio 0.94, interval 0.56 to 1.60. These are separate analyses, not interchangeable updates to one median. The indexed abstract reports overall-survival hazard ratio 1.07 and stratified P = .52. Fifty-six of sixty assigned to ablation received SBRT, about 93%; this was not BOOSTER's probe-based comparison. Table 1 has ten triple-negative participants among 125, 8%, and 99 with hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative cancer. The report does not precisely establish every subtype's effect, and confidence intervals crossing one do not prove zero effect. The authors' recommendation against routine use outside trials retains a separate palliation exception.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text:
Image-guided thermal ablation includes radiofrequency current, microwave fields and cryoablation. The applicator changes tissue temperature; injury depends on exposure through space and time. Chemical ablation and membrane-disrupting electrical approaches belong to a broader ablation category and should be named separately. These methods differ from ionising radiation.

Planning considers access, the target and intended margin, blood flow and nearby structures. Neither a central reading nor a visible treatment zone proves lethal exposure throughout the target. A study’s lesion-size rule is not a universal physical ceiling. Treatment can injure normal tissue and may require further procedures; outpatient treatment, preserved function and unlimited repeatability are not guaranteed.

The reporting consensus separates technical coverage, technique efficacy at a defined follow-up and later local progression. The method, assessment, retreatments and complications belong with each result. Local control or symptom relief does not establish eradication of disease elsewhere or a systemic immune benefit.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: BOOSTER studied ablation added to continuing immunotherapy in selected advanced lung cancer with limited residual disease after response. It was not an SBRT trial or a comparison in every metastatic setting. Cryo-versus-heating comparisons within that small trial were exploratory rather than a randomised test of the two modalities.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: Record the method, applicator settings such as power in watts, exposure time, measured temperature in degrees Celsius where relevant, and three-dimensional zone or margin measurements with the imaging method and assessment time. A generator setting or one sensor does not measure exposure everywhere or count viable cells.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: BOOSTER randomised 65 selected patients with residual advanced lung cancer after checkpoint treatment, rather than the planned 137; its primary analysis included 42 with ablation and twenty without. The primary progression-free-survival clock began at immunotherapy initiation, before randomisation, so its medians of 26.7 versus 11.7 months include a selected pre-entry period. The report separately gives a randomisation-clock analysis of 17.1 versus 4.4 months. These clocks cannot be exchanged when comparing headlines. The physician selected freezing or heating: the abstract says thirteen cryoablation and 31 thermal-ablation patients, whereas Figure 3 and the discussion say thirteen and 29 among the 42 analysed. The discussion also notes larger lesions in the thermal group and no correction for multiple comparisons. This internally discrepant, exploratory comparison does not establish universal superiority of freezing or an immune-optimal modality.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: Vanpouille-Box's 2017 experiments found that sufficiently high single radiation doses induced the DNA-degrading enzyme TREX1, reducing cytosolic DNA and interferon signalling. The threshold sufficient to clear cytosolic DNA varied from twelve to eighteen gray across the tested mouse and human carcinoma cell lines; a patient-derived lung-cancer xenograft was also examined. The work connected repeated lower-dose irradiation, type I interferon and dendritic-cell-dependent T-cell effects in defined models with checkpoint blockade. It does not supply a universal human dose ceiling, show that more physical injury always gives more useful immunity or select an individual radiation schedule.
anchors.sourceScope: Abstract and seven selected body passages read. Cell/model thresholds, not a human dose ceiling or selected schedule.

anchors.text:
A tumour specimen can contain malignant, immune, stromal and normal cells. A difference in an aggregate molecular signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells or both. That is different from a directly counted cell fraction or a density per sampled area, each of which also needs its denominator and sampled region.

Preparation can change what is recovered. Slyper and colleagues compared single-cell and single-nucleus profiling in matched tumour specimens and found similar cell types at sometimes different proportions. A recovered profile mixture is therefore not automatically the original tissue census. Deconvolution and purity models can help investigate contributions under assumptions; they do not certify the cell of origin of every signal or remove sampling differences.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: In a fictional assay using equal sampled areas and the same counting method, ten immune cells among fifty total cells is 20%, while ten among twenty is 50%. The immune count remains ten. Loss of other cells can raise the fraction without additional immune-cell entry; these observations alone do not establish recruitment, recognition or killing. This simple cell fraction is not the clinical stromal tumour-infiltrating-lymphocyte score, which has a different denominator.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: A second invented comparison starts with ten cells in one square millimetre of viable edge from lesion L. Follow-up A counts ten in the same stated area and region of L, giving ten cells per square millimetre at both times under the supplied assumptions. Follow-up B counts ten in 0.2 square millimetres from an injured centre of lesion M, giving fifty per square millimetre. B does not show a rise within L. Retain the lesion, viable area, centre or edge, collection time, treatment context and counting method. An early sample can capture transient injury signals and a later one a changed surviving-cell mixture. Equal area does not make separate tissue pieces identical, and matched sampling alone still cannot establish recruitment causation.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: Measurement layers ask different questions. Anatomical imaging describes structure; tracer imaging depends on the stated product and its distribution; immunohistochemistry localises a protein in sampled tissue; bulk RNA pools captured messages; receptor sequencing describes recovered sequences and their sampled abundances; and controlled recognition or killing assays test a specified function under their conditions. RNA abundance is not accessible surface protein. Formenti's lung-cancer radiation-plus-ipilimumab study used clinical, blood-repertoire and selected functional readouts together; none is a universal immune-success marker or a substitute for the other measurements.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text:
Biologically effective dose, or BED, is calculated from a radiation pattern and a specified tissue-and-endpoint model. In the basic equal-fraction linear-quadratic calculation, both total dose and dose per fraction matter, together with the assumed alpha/beta ratio. The result is a modelled quantity reported in gray, not extra physical dose.

EQD2 expresses the dose in two-gray fractions that would give the same modelled effect under the same assumptions. Neither expression is a universal conversion between any schedules. Repair, time, distribution and model validity must be considered for the actual irradiation pattern; numerical equivalence does not establish equivalent control or harm.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: For equal brief external-beam fractions, the basic linear-quadratic expression is BED = n × d × [1 + d/(alpha/beta)]. Here n is the count, d is dose per fraction in gray and alpha/beta is a tissue-and-endpoint parameter in gray, so the ratio inside the bracket is dimensionless. The simplified expression assumes negligible repair during delivery and complete repair between fractions, and omits overall time and repopulation. Prolonged or internally distributed irradiation needs additional modelling; this expression does not automatically compare every brachytherapy or radioligand pattern.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: Two invented patterns, fifteen fractions of two gray and five of six gray, each total thirty gray. At an assumed alpha/beta of three gray, their BED values are fifty and ninety gray; at an assumed ten gray, they are 36 and 48. The between-pattern difference is forty under the first assumption and twelve under the second. These assumed parameters are not measurements of a person's cancer or organs. Lower alpha/beta gives fraction size more weight at fixed total dose; a low-ratio tumour narrows a contrast inferred using a ten-gray tumour assumption.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text: Higher calculated BED means a larger modelled effect under the stated column's assumptions, rather than an observed benefit or toxicity probability. Dose distribution, exposed volume, intervals, overall duration, other exposures, population, comparator, endpoint and follow-up remain necessary. Arithmetic cannot validate extrapolation to a fraction size or settle parameter uncertainty. Five sessions do not identify stereotactic delivery, and this equation measures neither priming nor an abscopal response or immune threshold.
anchors.sourceScope: Current selected source passages and source-first reasoning at the recorded depth; no whole-document reading or independent acceptance.

anchors.text:
The linear-quadratic model expresses the surviving cell fraction after dose d as exp(-alpha × d - beta × d squared). The alpha/beta ratio is a parameter in gray for a specified tissue and endpoint. At fixed total physical dose, a lower ratio gives fraction size greater weight. Historical teaching values near ten gray for many tumours and early-responding tissues such as skin and mucosa, and three for late normal-tissue effects, are conventions rather than constants for every tumour or organ. A planned START-A/pilot meta-analysis estimated 4.6 gray for breast tumour control, with 95% confidence interval 1.1 to 8.1, and 3.4 for late photographic breast change, interval 2.3 to 4.5. The trialists interpreted these estimates as similar fraction-size sensitivity for breast cancer and its dose-limiting normal tissues.

The basic equal-fraction calculation assumes equal effects per fraction and complete repair between fractions and does not include overall treatment time. Too short an interval or slow repair can violate that assumption. Extrapolation to a large fraction size or prolonged irradiation needs assessment; a model calculation alone validates neither the pattern nor clinical equivalence.
anchors.sourceScope: START-A complete abstract and specified IAEA typeset pages read. Only the LQ assumptions, conventions and START estimates are used by this cohort; the retained final RBE paragraph is not newly source-verified.

anchors.text:
Hypofractionation uses larger doses per fraction relative to a stated conventional comparison, commonly with fewer treatments. Keep total gray, dose per fraction, count, spacing, overall duration and treatment volume together. For equal fractions, total physical dose is the fraction count multiplied by dose per fraction; this arithmetic does not establish biological equivalence. Acceleration changes overall timing; a boost changes the dose to a selected region. Hypofractionation does not by itself identify stereotactic delivery.

Biological response depends on tissue, repair and timing, rather than total physical dose alone. Alpha/beta is a model parameter in gray describing fraction-size sensitivity. Under the linear-quadratic model and its assumptions, a lower ratio predicts greater sensitivity to fraction size at the same total physical dose. Historical teaching values near 10 gray for early effects and 3 for late effects are conventions, not universal constants. A planned START-A/pilot meta-analysis estimated 4.6 gray for tumour control, with confidence interval 1.1 to 8.1, and 3.4 for late photographic breast change, with interval 2.3 to 4.5. Keep the model, endpoint and uncertainty.

START-B compared 50 gray in 25 fractions over five weeks with 40 in 15 over three weeks after surgery for early breast cancer, assessing local-regional relapse and late effects. FAST-Forward tested 40 gray in 15 fractions over three weeks against 27 or 26 in five over one week to the whole breast or chest wall. Its five-year report supported non-inferiority of 26 gray for breast relapse under the trial margin; 27 gray produced more normal-tissue effects. These results do not validate every five-visit course, nodal field, reirradiation plan or immune-priming schedule.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text: FAST-Forward randomised 4,096 people after surgery for early breast cancer to forty gray in fifteen fractions over three weeks, 27 in five over one week, or 26 in five over one week to the whole breast or chest wall. Its five-year report found 26 in five non-inferior for ipsilateral breast-tumour relapse under the prespecified margin; the five-year relapse estimate after forty gray was 2.1%. Normal-tissue assessments differed by regimen: 27 produced more effects, whereas 26 did not show that increase versus forty. These are local-control and normal-tissue results in the tested setting, not a demonstration that a five-visit course is SBRT or an immune optimum.
anchors.sourceScope: Complete five-year FAST-Forward abstract read, with literal less-than clauses preserved. No whole-paper or later-results claim.

anchors.text:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text:
Chen and Mellman’s 2013 framework describes seven linked steps: release of cancer antigens; their collection and presentation; T-cell priming and activation; trafficking; entry into tumour tissue; recognition of cancer cells; and killing. Further antigen release may support another round. In conventional T-cell recognition, a displayed peptide-HLA complex and a suitable T-cell receptor are separate dependencies.

This is a T-cell-centred organizing model, not a universal route, assay result or treatment-selection algorithm. Steps overlap, priming may occur away from the tumour, and other immune mechanisms require their own account. Checkpoints and local tissue conditions affect several steps. Vaccines aim to generate or expand reactive responses, checkpoint drugs interrupt selected inhibitory signals, and engineered cells provide a recognition system and effectors. Each still needs appropriate targets, access, function and safety evidence.
anchors.sourceScope: Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified.

anchors.text:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

anchors.text:
Local treatment can supply tumour antigens, and an adjuvant or other immune intervention may support their presentation and priming. The proposal needs evidence for each step and for useful immune effects in the relevant host and setting. It does not guarantee recognition of every antigen or every lesion.

Injury, danger signals, immune-cell changes, distant lesion responses and comparative patient outcomes are different observations. The actual local method and accompanying treatments must be named. A response during combined treatment does not isolate which component caused it.

anchors.text:
The 2020 consensus defines immunogenic cell death through the adaptive immune response, not merely the appearance of dead cells. Antigens, appropriately timed danger signals, antigen-presenting cells and a responsive host all matter. Apoptotic or other death machinery does not by itself classify the immune outcome.

Calreticulin exposure, ATP or HMGB1 release and interferon-related signals are useful mechanistic readouts, but none alone proves protective immunity. Functional cross-priming and appropriate in-vivo immune tests address later steps. The consensus distinguishes mouse vaccination models from established disease; neither a surrogate marker nor a positive mouse assay establishes clinical benefit in a person.
